The expansion of international trade agreements, which has been a defining feature of the post-war economic order, is perhaps best understood as both an engine of prosperity and a source of significant distributional inequity. It has been well documented that trade liberalization, while generating aggregate gains in economic output, has been associated with the displacement of workers in certain industries; the social costs of such displacement are arguably borne disproportionately by communities with limited capacity for economic adaptation. It is worth considering that the theoretical underpinnings of free trade, rooted as they are in the doctrine of comparative advantage, rest upon assumptions that may not hold in an era characterized by capital mobility and technological disruption. The negotiation of future trade arrangements, it is suggested, ought to incorporate provisions that more adequately address labor standards, environmental protections, and the equitable distribution of benefits. The failure to do so would perhaps risk further eroding public confidence in the institutions of global economic governance.
